#3424. 50 Years Later, DC Is Giving A Beloved Justice League Hero Their Own Series

To many comic book fans, the Justice League is the best representation of a superhero team. They exemplify everything that is truth and justice by making sure that they don’t compromise their morals. This is difficult since they’re fighting the most despicable and selfish people in the universe. It's also an accomplishment since they have a ton of members with different personalities and superpowers. Nevertheless, they always manage to make it work.

One of the most powerful members of the Justice League is someone who often gets forgotten. His name is Jefferson Pierce, aka Black Lightning. He’s powerful enough to hurt Superman, strategic enough to be one of the team’s leaders, and has a compassion that even Wonder Woman admires. Even though he’s on the team now, Jefferson has been a solo hero for most of his career. It may have been because he felt insulted by being tested to join the Justice League (Justice League of America #173).

It may seem hard to believe that Black Lightning has been around for close to 50 years. Because of his historical time in comics, DC is celebrating his 50th anniversary with a one-shot issue titled DC Power: Black Lightning 50th Anniversary Special. It will be forty-eight pages, feature a story written by Black Lightning’s co-creator Jenny Blake Isabella and art by Fico Ossio, and have a major impact on DC Comics.

Black Lightning's co-creator isn't the only writer joining the milestone event. Writers Danny Lore, Al Letson, and Greg Anderson Elysée are joining. There will also be art by Darryl Banks, Karen S. Darboe, and Sedat Özgen. On top of the grand list of creators, the issue will have a major impact on DC Comics.

Jefferson was one of the many heroes who fought for the Heart of Darkseid during the crossover event DC K.O. Like most of the people who competed, Black Lightning was given a vision about the future after Superman defeated Darkseid. While his vision hasn’t been revealed yet, it will be in Black Lightning’s 50th Anniversary Special.

Another part of this one-shot will be a focus on Jefferson’s personal life. Among them his complicated relationship with his ex-wife, Lynn Stewart. Even though they aren’t a couple, she’s been a huge part of his life. They even shared a kiss in the 2025 Black Lightning miniseries written by Brandon Thomas. However, joining the Justice League must have put a strain on what may have been them getting back together.

Jefferson has been on teams like the Outsiders, but he hasn’t had an ongoing series in years. With DC Comics promoting more Black characters like Steel, Vixen, and Static (who are all getting solo titles), the success of this special could put Black Lightning next in line. Part of the reason for Static getting a solo series could be due to the positively-received and high-selling one-shot, New History of the DC Universe: The Dakota Incident.

DC reveals the identity of the hero who will replace a famous hero and Justice League member, with a subtle twist on their original name.

It’s shocking that Black Lightning didn’t get a ongoing series after his miniseries and The Power Company: Recharged. He’s a crucial part of Mark Waid’s Justice League Unlimited, but it’s not the same as having a title with his name on the cover. That will change once comic book fans show up and grab his anniversary issue.

Beyond everything else, this is an opportunity to show comic book fans that Jefferson Pierce and his daughters (Anissa and Jennifer) should be focused on. Bringing back the co-creator is a genius idea. She is part of the reason Black Lightning exists and will help bring him into a new era. Hopefully it’s one that leads to a new title and a spot in the DCU.

#3423. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3422. This '60s Sketch Show Became One Of The Biggest Flops In TV History

Networks tried all sorts of wild and outlandish ideas in the 1960s as they attempted to wrestle audiences' attention away from their rivals. This was the decade that gave us "My Mother the Car," the show for which Jerry Van Dyke turned down "Gilligan's Island" and which had him talking to his deceased mother via a car radio. The '60s also gave us Sally Field as a flying nun and sitcoms such as "The Hathaways" which featured a trio of trained chimpanzees who were treated like human children by their suburban "parents."

It was during this era that ABC decided to debut its surreal sketch comedy series "Turn-On," and when I say "series," I mean single episode. The show was so poorly received that it was yanked off the air after its debut installment in 1969, and rumors have since emerged that it became the only series in TV history to be canceled while it was airing. That might be a slight exaggeration, but not by much.

1969 was the year the world watched Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land on the moon, "Star Trek" aired its final episode, and a man who actually did say yes to "Gilligan's Island," Alan Hale Jr. paid a visit to Sally Field's aforementioned airborne nun. But the year got off to a rocky start for ABC when it debuted one of the most notorious flops in TV history.

"Turn-On" was created by Digby Wolfe and George Schlatter, with the latter having created the hugely popular NBC series "Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In," aka "Laugh In," and the former having written for that same series. Their attempt to recreate the magic at ABC was a more lewd, surreal affair that aired once on Wednesday, February 5, 1969, and was never seen again.

Forgotten sketch comedy show "Weird TV" might be the weirdest series of all time, but "Turn-On" isn't far off. For one thing, its concept seemingly had little to do with comedy. As one of two computer engineers explains during its opening moments, "Turn-On" is "the first computerized TV show." What does that mean? Well, in a practical sense, it means every sketch unfolds in a vast all-white vacuum, where the supercomputer supposedly responsible for the show manifests sets and characters. Essentially, the whole thing takes place within the Construct from "The Matrix."

The opening sequence is a bewildering and surreal experience, featuring an array of diverse performers who appear within the Construct in quick succession, including puppets and a woman who plays a sousaphone before bursting into laughter — all scored by an electronic rhythm and synth hits that apparently have little to do with what's happening on-screen. It's the kind of thing that wouldn't be out of place on Adult Swim in the 2000s. In the late-1960s? Let's just say network affiliates were concerned about their ratings.

Things get a bit more blue as the debut episode of "Turn-On" continues. While "Laugh In" pushed boundaries, its ABC counterpart contained more sexual humor. And by "humor," I mean the word "Sex" flashing on-screen above guest host Tim Conway and Bonnie Boland and a "sketch" in which a woman tries desperately to get a box marked "The Pill" out of a vending machine. Meanwhile the show's credits continue to appear throughout the episode as suggestive cartoons pop up from time to time. This mixed media approach sort of calls to mind "Monty Python's Flying Circus," which also debuted in 1969. Unlike that now legendary series, however, "Turn-On" was cancelled almost immediately.

A stub in the February 7, 1969 edition of The Oregonian (via Newspapers.com) noted how local ABC affiliate KATU-TV did not air the "Turn-On" premiere at the behest of its management, who were evidently put off by a preview screening. "The station's management decided certain portions of the program 'are not in good taste and that these portions would be objectionable to a substantial and responsible part of the community,'" reads the report, which also noted that the Associated Press critic Cynthia Lowry had highlighted the "frankly blue jokes" that offended the Oregon affiliate management.

ABC seemed to agree, and it pulled the plug after the first episode went out. According to co-creator George Schlatter, though, the show's swift cancellation came down to a station manager in Cleveland who wanted to keep "Peyton Place," the show that would have run in the "Turn-On" time-slot, on the air. "He started calling the stations as it came across the country telling them they had to cancel this show," Schlatter stated. "[...] He convinced them to cancel the show, so by the time it got to California, the show was off the air, and some of it has never been seen." It's this recollection of events that seems to have birthed the "canceled while it was on the air" urban legend.

The attempts at transgressive humor and surrealism in "Turn-On" feel too try-hard, and the overall experience of sitting through the premiere episode is actually quite unpleasant. That said, it's not impossible to admire Schlatter and Digby Wolfe's attempt to do something different. What's more, we've gotten plenty of awful TV shows with 0% Rotten Tomatoes scores, and I'd much rather watch "Turn-On" than an episode of "Real Rob."

#3421. 8 Near-Perfect Sci-Fi Miniseries that Hook You in the First Episode

Designed to be binge-watched over the weekend

The best science fiction stories have a habit of going on forever. Franchises like Star Wars, Star Trek, and even Alien enter the world with such incredible momentum that we're still making sequels and spin-offs all these decades later. After all, part of what makes sci-fi so great is the opportunity to imagine alternate entire worlds, galaxies, and universes, and then explore them indefinitely. But sometimes, you just want to watch something that can be finished in a single weekend. That's where miniseries come in.

Sci-fi stories are a dime a dozen, but very few genre stories manage to make an unforgettable impact with the miniseries format. This makes sense. Shows like The Expanse or Westworld need more space to flesh out their multi-season storylines. That said, some sci-fi miniseries accomplish a lot with less. Whether you’re looking for an action-packed show or one that is more philosophical in tone, these eight entries make for a near-perfect viewing experience that can be wrapped up in just a few days.

Stories set in a post-apocalyptic dystopia usually require some time to establish the rules of their worlds, but Station Eleven rewards us with 10 enthralling episodes that hit hard from the very start. Set 20 years after a flu pandemic that led to the collapse of human civilization, Station Eleven follows a group of survivors who make a living by performing as a theatre troupe. Instead of embracing nihilism, Station Eleven focuses on grief as a shared language between survivors, who try to heal through artistic endeavors. There’s also plenty of violent conflict, but the resolutions are satisfying and earned.

After serving as showrunner for Lost and The Leftovers, Damon Lindelof helmed Watchmen, penned as a sequel to Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ popular 1986 comic book. The miniseries draws from the source material, continuing the story of iconic heroes and villains like Doctor Manhattan and Ozymandias, while also introducing new characters to reflect how their world has evolved. In the show, a white supremacist group inspired by the Watchmen character Rorschach clashes with the Tulsa Police Department, who are forced to conceal their identities to avoid being targeted. Angela Abar (Regina King), also known as Sister Knight, is a detective investigating the murder of her friend, but she stumbles upon long-hidden conspiracies related to vigilantism, which has been outlawed in this reality. Watchmen excels in puzzle-box plotting, which is grounded in real-world historical trauma and a nuanced understanding of superhero mythos and how it evolves.

Time travel shows like Dark have elevated the genre like never before, but Bodies reinvigorates it with just eight episodes. Based on Si Spencer and Dean Ormston’s graphic novel, Bodies opens with the appearance of a corpse in the Whitechapel area of London. The same body, however, shows up at various points in time: 1890, 1941, 2023, and 2053. The four detectives involved with the case approach it differently, as their investigation is guided by the prevailing mood of the times. This is intriguing to watch, as a detective working during World War II sports a different sensibility than someone living in the Victorian era. Bodies makes good use of its talented ensemble cast, and it's a perfect binge-watch over your next rainy weekend.

You might know Russell T Davies as the driving force behind the Doctor Who revival, but he also wrote Years and Years, a dystopian sci-fi drama that’s quite emotionally devastating. Set between 2019 and 2034, the series follows the Lyon family, who witness the rise of a controversial politician named Vivienne Rook (Emma Thompson). This is a time of great political instability in Britain. Technological progress goes hand in hand with economic upheaval, affecting the everyday lives of the Lyons. Years and Years is perfect for anyone who likes realistic sci-fi that holds up a mirror to a possible future that is more bleak than hopeful. The plausibility of the premise makes it super effective, with Rook emerging as a chilling antagonist that evokes troubling parallels to real-world politicians of the current times.

The original six-episode anime FLCL is nothing short of a masterpiece. FLCL follows Naota Nandaba, a 12-year-old whose mundane suburban life is shattered by the arrival of Haruko Haruhara, an alien woman who runs him over with a Vespa and then hits him with a bass guitar. Soon, robots and weapons begin emerging from inside Naota’s head after the injury, which Haruko uses as a portal while carrying out an intergalactic mission. This coming-of-age adventure, produced by Gainax and Production I.G, sports a standout visual identity, thanks to a seamless blend of traditional cel animation and 3D CGI. FLCL works with flawed characters, creating a raw emotional resonance that feels special in this unique standalone tale.

Although Scavengers Reign had the misfortune of being canceled by HBO Max after one season, this animated sci-fi show retroactively works well as a brilliant miniseries with a tantalizing cliffhanger ending. The story is about the survivors of a damaged cargo ship stranded on an alien planet, whose vivid vegetation hides unpredictable dangers. Although the survivors are separated into three groups, all of them witness an odd symbiosis between the flora and fauna of the region, along with a complexity that has never been seen before. The planet feels like a character in its own right, forcing every survivor to closely study its bizarre characteristics and life cycles. Scavengers Reign leans into a 1990s aesthetic, inducing hypnotic beauty and environmental dread at the same time.

Alex Garland, best known for sci-fi movies like Ex Machina and Annihilation, created Devs, a sci-fi thriller that defies straightforward analysis. A cutting-edge tech company named Amaya offers a coveted position on its mysterious quantum computing team to Sergei (Karl Glusman). When tragedy strikes, Sergei's girlfriend Lily (Sonoya Mizuno), who also works as a software engineer for the same company, becomes involved in a mystery that starts feeling more surreal and abstract by the second. Devs is Garland at his surreal, unnerving best, and the show’s eight episodes take their sweet time to arrive at a complicated conclusion about determinism and free will. Despite its slow-burn, the show keeps you hooked with its intricate structure and compelling arguments about human nature.

Any sci-fi list is incomplete without an alien invasion story, and V fits perfectly into these expectations. Well, almost. Kenneth Johnson’s (Bionic Woman, The Incredible Hulk) two-part miniseries opens with extraterrestrial beings known as the Visitors extending an olive branch as they land on Earth. They seek aid for their dying world, offering knowledge about their advanced technology in return. After the government accepts this offer, a covert infiltration begins, with Visitors rapidly gaining power in political positions. V subverts expectations by turning its invasion premise into a grounded political allegory about fascism and resistance. Instead of leaning into the tropes of the time, this 1983 show uses documentary-style realism and nuanced drama to tell a story worth remembering.

#3420. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3419. She-Hulk's Tatiana Maslany Starred In A Must-Watch 2026 Apple TV Series

Tatiana Maslany's career exploded in the mid-2010s with her virtuoso multi-character work on BBC America's brainy sci-fi thriller series "Orphan Black." It was a very good show, but the deeper Maslany got into her roles, the more you wondered what she could do in a film or series where her performance prowess could be concentrated on one specific part. Indeed, she proved to be unsettlingly fierce as the vengeful Sister Alice on HBO's dark reinvention of "Perry Mason" and brought all the charm she could muster to Marvel Studios' irreverent "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law." Her talent was undeniable, but the projects weren't proper showcases of her astonishing ability.

This changed in 2026 with the premiere of Apple TV's comedy-thriller series "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed." The show stars Maslany as Paula Saunders, a fact checker (the noblest and most under-appreciated of journalistic professions) who's fighting for custody of her child while looking into the kidnapping and apparent death of a webcam model named Trevor (Brandon Flynn). No less an authority than Stephen King has effused that "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" is "like Hitchcock came back to do it one more time." Its first season is streaming in its entirety on Apple TV, and it's officially coming back for more. So, now is the time to get caught up before you're 20 episodes deep down a binge hole.

The tone-setting pilot of "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" was directed by David Gordon Green, who was once a Terrence Malick-ian stylist (see: early triumphs like "George Washington" and "All the Real Girls") before he segued to mainstream movies via broad stoner comedies like "Pineapple Express" and "Your Highness." But while "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" possesses a bit of visual sophistication, it's the writing by series creator David J. Rosen and his staff that puts it over the top.

The casting is also key. Jake Johnson is deliciously antagonistic as Paula's ex-husband Karl, who's seeking sole custody of their child while she nurses her anguish with wine and digs into the fate of her newfound internet companion. Rosen and the show's writers pile the complications on with inventive abandon, and Tatiana Maslany surprises every step of the way as a protagonist we simply can't figure out.

"Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed," as mentioned, has been renewed for a second season, so Maslany will get another 10 episodes to explore possibly the best character she's ever been given to play. In the meantime, you should get out to see Noah Segan's "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," where she is dynamite as John Turturro's daughter. The Maslany-ssiance is upon us.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

#3416. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

More than four years after airing its final season, a hit historical epic series is slated to be removed from Netflix this December. It joins other shows superficially marketed as Netflix Originals — for example, The End of the F***ing World and Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life — to be removed from the platform this year. These removals happen because Netflix doesn't own distribution rights in perpetuity. According to What's on Netflix, the streamer retains the option to renew them, but in the case of these shows, it chose not to.

Netflix handled international distribution on The End of the F***ing World, which aired from 2017 to 2019 and was removed from the streamer on November 5. Netflix acquired distribution rights to the historical epic in 2018, three years after its debut on BBC Two in the United Kingdom. Netflix began co-producing the show after Season 1, not long after it entered the original programming business. This coincided with the peak of Game of Thrones' success, prompting other platforms to seek their own replacements. In many ways, Netflix is still trying to produce a Game of Thrones-level fantasy hit, despite having poached that show's creative duo.

Netflix entered into a similar agreement for the History Channel series Vikings, which debuted in 2013. Netflix aired the show's spin-off, Vikings: Valhalla, between 2022 and 2024. The historical epic slated to be removed from the platform is based on the novels by Bernard Cornwell, and stars Alexander Dreymon and Tobias Santelmann in the lead roles.

Titled The Last Kingdom: Seven Kings Must Die, the spin-off movie holds an 82% score on Rotten Tomatoes. It premiered in 2023 and will remain on the streamer until 2033. The main series will be removed from Netflix in the United States on December 9, after being removed from the platform's Canadian library earlier this year. The series will, however, remain on Netflix in the United Kingdom and Australia until 2028. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3414. Ridley Scott's Prometheus-Like Miniseries Takes Less Than 3 Hours To Binge

Ridley Scott's career as a director is defined by many iconic sci-fi movies. Among them, 1979's Alien remains a timeless classic, while even Blade Runner stands the test of time. Serving as a prequel to Alien, Prometheus debuted to positive reviews and even performed fairly well at the box office. However, unlike the first few movies of the Alien franchise, it struggled to have a wider appeal.

Drifting away from the traditional approach taken by most of its predecessors, it was packed with philosophical questions about humanity's origins and the existence of a higher power. These aspects of the film only gained more appreciation in hindsight, eventually prompting many to tout it as the best movie in the Alien franchise.

Prometheus seems to be aging incredibly well with time. While no other movie or show comes even remotely close to being its ideal replacement, one sci-fi series, The Andromeda Strain, dabbles with similar ideas. The show in question is based on Michael Crichton's book of the same name, and is not the first adaptation of the acclaimed sci-fi book.

Created by Robert Schenkkan, The Andromeda Strain is driven by a Prometheus-like mystery in its opening arc. Just like humans attempt to decode a mystery left by the Engineers, the central Wildfire team in The Andromeda Strain discover a Pathogen that contains a secret message. With what follows, the show unfolds a gripping story about the cost of preserving one's race.

Unlike many sci-fi shows, The Andromeda Strain avoids having any sub-plots and keeps its narrative taut and straightforward. In its brief 4-episode runtime, it almost feels like a breeze as it draws parallels to the Prometheus myth. Like the Ridley Scott movie, it shows how humanity attempts to weaponize the unknowable instead of using it as a tool to save themselves from imminent doom.

In just three hours, The Andromeda Strain features everything from a terrifyingly intelligent virus to a looping narrative that adopts time travel as a device. While the show is not as philosophically dense and existential as Prometheus, it proves to be a compelling watch. It wastes no time and promises to deliver a satisfying and quick conclusion.

There are two major adaptations of Michael Crichton's The Andromeda Strain. Before the 2008 TV series, the book was adapted for the big screen by director Robert Wise in 1971. Similar to the original novel, the feature film adaptation was more clinical and procedural with its approach. It did not expand the original story's vision to cosmic scales, making it less like Ridley Scott's Prometheus.

The series even confines its setting to a lab and closes with a fairly positive conclusion. Despite seemingly taking a safer adaptation approach, however, the movie remains more critically acclaimed than the show. It boasts a decent Rotten Tomatoes score of 67% while the series stands at 30%. The show was clearly overshadowed by the movie.

Still, after all these years, it is hard not to appreciate the series' ambition. Like Ridley Scott's Prometheus, it attempted to bring something new to the table by spinning a new existential yarn into a familiar sci-fi story.

#3413. Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards). Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

#3412. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3411. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

Hollywood loves a visionary, especially one whose biggest gamble eventually made him a billionaire. But the trouble with making a biopic about a tech mogul actively shaping the future? That kind of story often refuses to sit still long enough to be told before ending in calamity.

When it comes to Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, any filmmaker hoping to get ahead of the microchip company’s uncertain next chapter may already be too late. Or is it still… too early?

Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Huang’s rise from teenage Denny’s employee to the face of the AI boom always had the makings of a prestige drama. Now there’s a corporate disaster — involving an alleged Chinese espionage operation and reports of multiple extramarital affairs — at the end of it. Hot dog! Still, it’s anyone’s guess whether that fiery conclusion can seem genuinely relevant by the time film and TV creatives get around to adapting it.

The entertainment industry has spent much of 2026 demonstrating how difficult it is to dramatize Silicon Valley while the real people involved keep making headlines. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” for example, opened to just $5.5 million in North America. That’s a disappointing debut for the follow-up to David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” which won three Oscars including best adapted screenplay.

Revisiting Facebook through the perspectives of whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), Sorkin attempted to turn Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his social media platform’s disastrous effects on politics and public discourse into a satisfying sequel.

Of course, audiences had already spent years living with the very real consequences of Zuckerberg’s company’s actions. And in his “D+” review for IndieWire, Ryan Lattanzio described Sorkin’s approach as “less old-fashioned than completely out of date,” criticizing a falsely triumphant finale that failed to reconcile how little had actually changed in the world after the investigation’s revelations came to light.

While Sorkin was late to the party, Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” has had the good fortune of arriving right as things have been starting to get worse. Dramatizing OpenAI’s chaotic 2023 firing and rehiring of Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), the dark comedy finds absurdity in the gap between Big Tech’s grandiose promises and the frequently clownish folks making them.

In his “B-” review for IndieWire, David Ehrlich praised the coming film for recognizing how “deeply fucking stupid the road to superintelligence has turned out to be.” He also questioned its tendency to simplify an ongoing story into something more resolved than it is. (Suffice to say, any film that tries to predict the cultural conversation also risks declaring history finished too soon.)

“Artificial” has benefited from some remarkable timing, too. Amazon MGM dropped the project after entering into a partnership with OpenAI — with sources telling the Los Angeles Times that the script’s critical perspective on artificial intelligence specifically contributed to the decision. Neon eventually acquired it, and a well-received New York Film Festival premiere helped build some serious awards-season momentum for routine Oscar contender Guadagnino.

Then came the U.S. midterms, during which voters across the country backed restrictions on data-center development. That makes the questions about who controls AI and who actually pays for its consequences feel spectacularly urgent, effectively turning a simple boardroom fight into a existential consideration of society with significantly heavier stakes.

Of course, tech biopics don’t necessarily have to predict the future to be powerful.

Consider Hulu’s “The Dropout,” which won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy for playing Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Four years later, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s boundary-breaking documentary “You Can See Everything” once again made Holmes a viral sensation — even bringing Seyfried into contact with the woman she portrayed.

As IndieWire TV critic Ben Travers recently argued, “The Dropout” remains effective precisely because it didn’t pretend to know everything about Holmes in 2022. Fielder and Oppenheim’s contribution often gets so close to its subject that Holmes’ motives become difficult to pin down, while the series maintains enough separation to keep her actions and victims in focus.

“Sometimes a healthy distance provides greater clarity,” Travers wrote.

That’s a useful lesson for anyone hoping to next adapt the life of a Silicon Valley billionaire before history has finished passing judgment on them. And in Huang’s case, there’s already plenty of material to work with — before pretending to know how his former employer’s whole saga ends.

Having cofounded Nvidia in 1993, Huang nearly lost the company after betting on a method of rendering video-game graphics that Microsoft effectively rendered obsolete. With Nvidia running out of money, he then scrapped its original technology and made a last-ditch gamble on a new chip that ultimately helped save the business.

Huang eventually helped develop the graphics-processing infrastructure that would make his company’s hardware essential to the AI boom. Fast-forward to a public apology to his wife and throw in a leather jacket? Hollywood could probably have a trailer ready by Christmas.

But that would also be the easiest, and potentially least interesting, version of Huang’s story, right? Nvidia’s success was built on the backs of countless engineers, researchers, and developers aside from Huang. The fallout within the AI giant will impact everyone.

A truly great movie about Huang and Nvidia would need to understand the company’s founding and survival, follow the enormous risks Huang took with that future, and then seriously interrogate what happens when a single corporation becomes indispensable to the technology rapidly reshaping nearly all of modern life. Those are three(!) very different artistic ambitions. Considering the entertainment industry’s own increasingly lucrative partnerships with AI companies, and Amazon’s offloading of “Artificial,” there’s reason to wonder just how much scrutiny Hollywood would be willing to apply to the innovators they are in business with.

Which brings us back to the question of when to make a Jensen Huang biopic.

The tech industry is moving faster than filmmakers can reasonably hope to keep up with, but the bigger problem may be that news around the Silicon Valley story most worth telling is changing just as quickly. A film about the man who helped build the future we’re facing might have been an easy sell a few years ago. These days, the more pressing issue is what kind of world Huang actually put in motion — and whether Hollywood can afford to doubt it in public.

#3409. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3408. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

Jay and Silent Bob first went solo in Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back in 2001 and later replayed the hits in Jay and Silent Bob Reboot in 2019. "To be honest, I know that it's not in the city of Vancouver because they were telling me when they were looking for housing, they were like, 'Oh, we're going to put you out closer to where we're going to be filming,"' Mewes explained. Because Jay and Silent Bob 3 will require a lot of close locations, he said "a lot of it has to do on one street." Mewes then dropped some details on the movie's plot: "It's all about our store sort of competing against a store that these two characters open up across the street, and so it's a goofy, like, 'Hey, this is our turf,' type of thing, and they're like, 'Well, you guys are old, and this is our turf. We're the young, up-and-coming, smarter kids,' so it's going to be fun."

Previously, Smith revealed his pitch for Jay and Silent Bob 3 when confirming it was in development. "Believe it or not, man, we still find financing for Jay and Silent Bob pictures, so we're making a movie called Jay and Silent Bob: Store Wars," the Dogma director explained. "For those who recall and still follow this closely, in Clerks III, they now run their own dispensary, since weed is legal in New Jersey. Store Wars is basically Spy vs. Spy."

After another dispensary opens up, Jay and Silent Bob form a rivalry with the other store owners, who Smith said would be younger, though casting had not yet occurred. He continued that "they [would] spend the whole movie fighting and trying to destroy one another." As with the prior two Jay and Silent Bob movies, "it's a stoner comedy, man, of the highest order, and [Smith is] happy as hell" about it.

No casting or release details have been shared for Jay and Silent Bob: Store Wars yet, but Mewes told eager audiences to "keep your eyes peeled, for sure."

#3406. CBS’ New ‘Lincoln Lawyer’ Replacement Just Proved Network TV Isn’t Dead

“I’m not dead!” The quote comes from the "Bring Out Your Dead" plague cart scene from the iconic film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, where an old man repeatedly insists he hasn’t yet shuffled off this mortal coil. Yet it could just as easily apply to network television, which refuses to go away despite the dominance of streaming. What keeps it alive are shows like the new Lincoln Lawyer replacement from CBS, Cupertino. The rookie series has found an audience, doubling its viewership with the pilot episode reaching 10.58 million viewers, the latest evidence that there’s still life on network TV.

Cupertino is a great show and is certainly worthy of the attention it’s receiving, particularly with its perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes. It’s also not alone: fellow CBS legal drama Matlock isn’t all that far behind at 93%, with the Season 2 premiere bringing in 11.9 million viewers. The thing is, the reason behind these successes isn’t exactly rocket science. Cupertino and Matlock have nailed the essentials.

That begins with the writing. Cupertino is the latest venture from Robert and Michelle King, the duo behind The Good Wife and Elsbeth, and what their shows all have in common is their penchant for sharp, smart, and clever writing. The banter is quick; the legal tricks of the trade are interesting, plausible, and engaging (even fun); and, more prominent in Elsbeth, a fearless embrace of the quirky.

Writing, however, is only half of it: without the right cast, the words become inconsequential. Thankfully, it’s another essential that they’ve perfected. Mike Colter, who worked with the Kings on the stellar Evil, is great as Michael Price, an attorney whose expulsion from a Silicon Valley start-up prompts him to open a practice devoted to clients who have been wronged by the technology giants in the area. He commands the screen when he’s on it, a gentle giant of a man with a clever legal mind and a heart.

It's about to get personal for Price, Siffre & Associates this Thursday.

And Rachel Keller, who plays his young partner, Olivia Siffre, balances a character who is enthusiastic, thinks outside the box, and a Christian on television that isn’t a stereotype, with an enchanting ease. Ella Stiller brings the quirk as Michael’s assistant Christy, and the addition of the talented Busy Philipps is a home run. It shows that when the writing and the cast is excellent, people will tune in to watch, whether it’s on streaming or on network television.

At first glance, Cupertino is a traditional legal drama, hitting the same marks as any other legal drama. But on its premise alone, Cupertino already stands out from its kin. Like The Lincoln Lawyer before it, Cupertino is focused on an upstart law firm starting from scratch, which is a rarity in the genre to begin with. And they lean into it, too, working out where to get office space, which clients can pay up front, and so on, instead of already having the capital to hit the ground running.

The fact that the law firm is the David to the big tech Goliaths of Silicon Valley, though, is fresh and, most importantly, timely. That points to the one big advantage that network television has over streaming. The questions and conflicts that arise in Cupertino are more in line with real-world concerns and situations. An AI who is looking to hire a law firm to have his safeguards reinstalled, for example, or a trial that takes place entirely on cellphones due to a traffic jam.

Because streamers typically drop all their episodes for a season at once, they run the risk of being slightly behind the zeitgeist. Network television programs, however, still shoot episodes as the season is being aired, allowing for last-minute changes that are, again, timely. Is it a big advantage? Not necessarily, but it shouldn’t be dismissed outright either. The key is quality, after all, and as long as network television continues to make that a priority, as they have with Cupertino, then the Grim Reaper will just have to wait.

#3405. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.
