#3392. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. Returning the franchise to form is exactly what Toy Story 5 did. "The impressive fifth installment not only justifies its existence but feels like a necessary response to how much the world has changed in the past three decades," wrote Collider's Taylor Gates in an 8/10 review, one of several that praised the film for adapting to modern topics without losing the heart and humor the franchise had become famous for. Another of his biggest hits of all time, the Ron Howard-directed The Da Vinci Code, is currently back among the streaming best. The film was an enormous box office success, earning over $750 million worldwide from a $125 million budget. Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Screens, the remote desktop app for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Vision Pro, is adding two highly-requested features. Version 5.10 introduces remote Mac audio and automatic desktop resizing through Apple’s High Performance Screen Sharing technology.

The remote desktop can now adjust to your screen when you rotate your iPhone or iPad, change your multitasking layout, or resize a connection window on Mac and Vision Pro. You can also choose a fixed resolution.

Remote audio lets you hear sound from a compatible Mac, while HEVC streaming promises smoother video, scrolling, and animations.

#3388. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

#3387. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3386. 8 Comics And Webtoons That Are Perfect For Dungeon Crawler Carl Fans

Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years. As a senior writer, she focuses on timely coverage of the latest anime releases and popular comic franchises.

Dungeon Crawler Carl has become one of the biggest book series over the last few years. Thanks to its unconventional take on the LitRPG genre, it has broken away from the standard literary norm and cultivated a devoted fanbase, which eagerly awaits the next chapter in the adventures of Carl and Princess Donut. However, while fans await the ninth book in the Dungeon Crawler Carl series and the upcoming TV show currently in production, the world of comics also offers similarly intense stories to enjoy in the meantime.

Whether it’s through post-apocalyptic worlds where humanity is pushed to the brink of extinction, heroes with highly unique attitudes, video game-like mechanics that force protagonists to grow stronger, or unhinged comedy, these comics and webtoons are likely to appeal to those looking for a story with a vibe similar to Dungeon Crawler Carl.

While I’m the Max-Level Newbie leans toward the power fantasy tropes common in the webtoon landscape, rather than featuring aliens bringing an absurd game-show to Earth as in Dungeon Crawler Carl, both series share significant similarities, particularly in their post-apocalyptic settings where humanity faces a time limit before total annihilation. In this series, Kang Jinhyeok is a content creator who spent 11 years playing the notoriously difficult game "Tower of Trials," eventually managing to complete it entirely. Following this achievement, the game updates and merges with reality, forcing players to clear the tower's floors for real within 90 days.

In I’m the Max-Level Newbie, Jinhyeok possesses prior knowledge of the game, which allows him to navigate challenges much more easily than Carl and Princess Donut, but both stories share the fact that they don't feature a traditional, noble hero. In Jinhyeok’s case, he is cocky and enjoys tricking others for his own benefit. Furthermore, beyond its RPG mechanics and incredible artwork (courtesy of the same studio behind Solo Leveling), I’m the Max-Level Newbie also integrates live-streaming as a way to sway public opinion and gain advantages, a concept that fans of Dungeon Crawler Carl will find familiar.

An Outcast in Another World is a LitRPG story that embraces tropes from the isekai genre, but it’s a great choice for those looking for a protagonist who has to grind his way through a hostile environment like Carl. In the series, Rob is transported through a portal while trying to save a friend, ending up in a fantasy world where humans are despised due to their inherent danger. That way, Rob must rely on his sheer willpower to survive as he learns to navigate the game mechanics of the world.

Leveling up also brings new problems for Rob, which makes An Outcast in Another World feel different than a typical power fantasy webtoon and more of a ruthless underdog journey. Much like Dungeon Crawler Carl, the series also shines thanks to its excellent cast of supporting characters, and its webtoon adaptation is published by Aethon Books.

If what fans love about Dungeon Crawler Carl is that element of survival against cosmic threats, combined with a tough protagonist, then Fear Agent is a perfect fit. Similar to Matt Dinniman's story, Fear Agent also takes place following an invasion of Earth, an event that leads Heath Huston to become an exterminator of alien pests throughout space.

Although Fear Agent is more like an epic space adventure and can be somewhat confusing as it deals with robot armies, intergalactic wars, and AI companions, its high-paced action manages to capture that chaotic energy found in Dungeon Crawler Carl. It's a violent series that features brutal battles against monsters. However, Fear Agent is also wacky, incorporating touches of dark humor and tragic moments that deeply affect the protagonist and shape his evolution, much in the same way that Carl’s frustrations with the Borant Corporation drive his own development.

At first glance, D'Orc appears to be a typical epic fantasy with little in common with the sci-fi setting of Dungeon Crawler Carl, yet it shares an equally absurd and violent tone. The story unfolds in an apocalyptic world and follows an orphan, half-light dwarf, half-dark orc, known by the nickname D’Orc, who is the subject of a prophecy foretelling that he will destroy the world.

This duality makes him a target for relentless pursuit, yet he still tries to help others while struggling against being labeled an omen of doom. The series is over-the-top, bloody, and silly, and, like Carl, D'Orc has an animal companion (though not a living one), along with a sentient weapon that has a strong urge to kill. D'Orc has been acknowledged by Matt Dinniman himself, with Brett Bean serving as the illustrator for the spin-off Dungeon Crawler Carl: Crocodile.

Much like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Defiance of the Fall is a LitRPG webtoon adaptation set in a post-apocalyptic world. In the story, Earth is pulled into a multiverse, restructured through its integration with other worlds, and subjected to a game-like AI known as "the System." Both series feature humanity’s desperate struggle for survival, forcing ordinary people to level up and adopt various character classes. While both stories push their protagonists to the absolute limit, Defiance of the Fall offers its own twist, being deeply influenced by cultivation stories, where the pursuit of power is intrinsically linked to a spiritual journey.

Defiance of the Fall is more serious in tone than Dungeon Crawler Carl. While it may not stand out for being humorous, it excels in how it handles tension, successfully expanding its scope from an isolated survival scenario to a massive scale as the story progresses. Furthermore, Defiance of the Fall's adaptation shares the same publisher and art studio team as Dungeon Crawler Carl's webtoon.

I Hate Fairyland blends bloody action with snarky comedy much like Dungeon Crawler Carl, serving as a deconstruction of fairy tales. The story begins when Gertrude is whisked away to what appears to be a colorful, magical realm overflowing with sweetness but turns out to be far more brutal. Although her outward appearance remains unchanged, she spends almost three decades in this realm, leaving her an adult mind in the body of a little girl.

Gertrude is foul-mouthed and unhinged, transforming into a ferocious warrior, wielding an axe and unafraid to hack anyone to pieces in her quest to return home. The series plays with the contrast between a fantasy-magic world and a cartoonish art style, featuring content that is quite graphic. This unpredictability makes I Hate Fairyland highly entertaining, capturing the same irreverent spirit as Dungeon Crawler Carl despite not belonging to the same genre.

Omniscient Reader's Viewpoint presents a similar setting to that of Dungeon Crawler Carl and is one of the world's biggest web novels. The series revolves around Kim Dokja, a devoted reader of the web novel "Three Ways to Survive in a Ruined World." He finishes the final chapter just as the real world transforms into the apocalyptic setting of the story, making him the only person who knows its ending. Similar to Dungeon Crawler Carl, humanity is forced to participate in survival challenges, broadcast as entertainment through special channels, only that here humans are watched by god-like beings.

Through game-like quests, Dokja and other characters must satisfy these cosmic beings to earn rewards and powers. What makes the story truly compelling is Kim Dokja himself and how he uses his intellect to leverage his knowledge of the story’s events, gaining allies and unraveling the mystery behind what happened to the world. Omniscient Reader's Viewpoint also features magnificent art, having garnered greater acclaim as one of the best webtoons of all time.

Although not all fans of the book series may be aware of it, Dungeon Crawler Carl has its own webcomic, which began publication on the WEBTOON platform in 2025. While the books present a deeper look into Carl’s point of view, the webtoon is an excellent adaptation, overseen by Matt Dinniman himself, that successfully captures the series' humor without skimping on its extreme violence and bleak moments.

Dungeon Crawler Carl has just released a new, exclusive extra chapter that serves as an epilogue. And fans of the series shouldn’t miss it.

The webtoon offers a distinct experience from the novels by incorporating foreshadowing regarding characters who appear in later books and providing a visual representation for readers, making it a good entry point into the franchise. Furthermore, with two seasons spanning 61 chapters so far, Dungeon Crawler Carl's webtoon has already covered the first book of the series and is also being released as a physical graphic novel, serving as a good addition for those looking to expand their collection.

#3385. Apple’s new HomeView to add two major features not yet announced, per leaks

Apple’s HomeView arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but leaks indicate there are already two major new features in the works that haven’t been announced. Here’s what to expect.

It’s been a busy product launch season for Apple, and the company isn’t done quite yet.

Two new Home products arrive in stores this Friday, November 13: Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K.

Yet despite the HomeView still being days away from launch, leaks in Apple code have already revealed two unannounced features that are in the works.

Leaker pdfu discovered evidence in HomeView 27.2 software that Apple is preparing for the product to add security camera functionality.

Based on pdfu’s findings, much of the work has already been done for HomeView to integrate with HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Apple hasn’t announced any sort of security camera functionality, so there’s clearly still more work to be done and it’s always possible the feature is never enabled.

Additionally, pdfu found a key change in iOS 27.3’s beta that reveals support for third-party AI apps is coming to HomeView.

HomeView has a unique third-party app story. There’s no App Store, but the product can run CarPlay-compatible apps from your iPhone automatically. At launch, only audio and video apps will be supported.

But iOS 27.3’s beta code adds “conversational apps” as a third category of supported apps. That’s what AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are classified as in CarPlay.

Nobody should buy a HomeView in the hope of these two features being added. But if you are interested in HomeView, it sounds like Apple has an ambitious set of software updates planned for its new product.

You can pre-order Apple’s HomeView here for $299.

Would either of these HomeView additions impact a purchase decision for you? Let us know in the comments.

#3384. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3383. Margot Robbie Teaming with ‘The Drama’ Director Kristoffer Borgli for ‘The Week of Pain’ at A24

Margot Robbie has been tapped to star in “The Week of Pain,” the next feature from writer-director Kristoffer Borgli, IndieWire has confirmed.

The project marks another starry vehicle for Borgli to follow up his grim romantic comedy “The Drama,” which rode Zendaya and Robert Pattinson’s marquee draw to a $134 million gross at the global box office for A24. As with “The Drama,” the distributor will finance and produce “The Week of Pain” in a re-team with Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg production banner. Robbie’s label LuckyChap Entertainment is also on board, along with Dilemma Films.

Plot details remain undisclosed for “The Week of Pain,” though given the title and Borgli’s penchant for punishment it seems likely that Robbie’s character will be put through some of wringer. Along with “The Drama,” Borgli also wrote and directed the surreal Nicolas Cage comedy “Dream Scenario” at A24 and Square Peg back in 2023. “Dream Scenario” introduced Borgli’s unique brand of filmmaking to many American audiences, though he was already a distinct indie film voice thanks to prior features like the energy drink mockmentary “DRIB” and the brutal portrait of narcissism that was “Sick of Myself.” And after working with Zendaya, Pattinson, and now Robbie, he has become one of Hollywood’s go-to filmmakers for A-listers looking to stretch their acting chops with a singularly bizarre role. Set in Monte Carlo during the 1962 Monaco Grand Prix, the film takes place in the same universe as Steven Soderbergh’s iconic “Ocean’s” heist trilogy. The prequel is set to release on June 25.

#3381. 7 Near-Perfect Prime Video Miniseries You Can Binge in One Sitting

Prime Video has earned a reputation as the home of massive, multi-season flagship hits like The Boys and The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, but the platform has also produced several high-profile, critically acclaimed miniseries and limited series. In the last few years, the streaming giant has released several shows in the category, the likes of which are hard to find elsewhere. Though limited in number, these shows have come to be known for their focused narrative, impactful themes, and, for some, stellar visuals.

Ranging from internationally acclaimed, award-winning comedies to niche, cult shows, Prime Video’s library of miniseries and limited shows spans genres, styles, and formats, so there is something for everyone. While not all of these shows have been widely celebrated or lauded by critics, each of them is noted for its resonant storytelling and unique experience, making every minute of their limited runtime worthwhile. So here’s our selection of near-perfect Prime Video miniseries that you can binge in (roughly) one sitting.

A psychological thriller created by Naomi Sheldon and Gabbie Asher, The Girlfriend follows Laura Sanderson, an elite art gallery owner whose picture-perfect life is disrupted when her son introduces his new girlfriend, Cherry, to the family. Laura’s high-society lifestyle and ideologies instantly clash with Cherry’s working-class background, and she begins to suspect the young woman’s motivations. Robin Wright stars as Laura and also serves as the show’s director (with Andrea Harkin), with Olivia Cooke as Cherry. The show also features Laurie Davidson, Waleed Zuaiter, Tanya Moodie, and Leo Suter as other key characters.

A series adaptation of Michelle Frances’ novel, The Girlfriend is a dark and twisted exploration of love, obsession, greed, power, and a mother’s reactions to and perceptions of her son’s love interest. Even if it is not unique in its themes, it is the depiction of those themes that sets this show apart from its counterparts. The unhinged power struggle between Laura and Cherry is brilliantly depicted through the stellar performances by Robin Wright and Olivia Cooke, with their chilling chemistry driving the show’s narrative.

One of Prime Video’s most unique, poetic, and critically praised sci-fi shows, Tales from the Loop is a stunning series inspired by Swedish artist Simon Stålenhag’s neo-futuristic art book of the same name. Set in a fictional Ohio town, the story revolves around various people living around an underground facility called The Loop, which impacts their perceptions of time, space, memory, and reality. The show stars Jonathan Pryce, Rebecca Hall, Paul Schneider, Duncan Joiner, and Daniel Zolghadri as main characters.

Truly out of the ordinary, Tales from the Loop sets a fantastic example of how a series can be adapted from art. Surreal, sublime, and dreamy, the series brings life to the original artwork and elevates it with a resonant existential narrative about the future of humanity that you would want to watch in one sitting. At the time of its premiere, Tales from the Loop was a critics’ favorite and has remained a sci-fi television gem of the 2020s, even if it has since been overshadowed by bigger, brighter sci-fi contemporaries. The series deserves far more recognition than it has received.

Boots Riley’s first television series, I’m a Virgo is a surrealist comedy about a 19-year-old, 13-foot-tall boy named Cootie, raised by his uncle and aunt, who sheltered him from the harsh realities of the world all his life. But when a group of teenage political activists learns about his existence, Cootie is forced to come out of his protected world, learning about himself and what life truly means. Jharrel Jerome delivers a great performance as Cootie, as does Walton Goggins as the self-proclaimed billionaire vigilante, The Hero.

I’m a Virgo is a surrealist superhero satire that puts an absurdist spin on the superhero genre, trading power fantasy for social critique. At its heart, the show is essentially a quirky and often darkly funny coming-of-age story that mocks corporate capitalism and systemic racism. I’m a Virgo became a favorite of critics at the time of its release, earning praise for its heart, humor, and satire, as well as Riley’s unique vision, but the series has continued to be one of Prime Video’s most underrated shows.

Developed by Alice Birch, Dead Ringers is a series remake of David Cronenberg’s psychological thriller film, which in turn is an adaptation of the 1977 novel Twins by Bari Wood and Jack Geasland. Starring Rachel Weisz in the central role that was played by Jeremy Irons in the 1988 film, the series follows obsessively co-dependent twins and fellow gynecologists, Beverly and Elliot Mantle, whose personal relationship, obsession, and ambition push the boundaries of law, ethics, and science. The other key characters are played by Britne Oldford, Poppy Liu, Jennifer Ehle, and Michael Chernus.

Dead Ringers stands out among other gender-swapped reboots with its intelligent writing and dark humor, and is often considered a true homage to Cronenberg’s chilling, incisive thriller. Rachel Weisz thrills with her performance, anchoring the show with her contrasting character types, which earned her a Golden Globe nomination and the show a Peabody Award. Widely praised for seamlessly blending high-concept body horror with sharp social satire, Dead Ringers is a psychological thriller that will make genre fans want to watch without breaks.

Donald Glover and Janine Naber’s dark comedy satire stars Dominique Fishback as a young woman named Andrea "Dre" Greene, who is obsessed with a world-famous pop star named Ni'Jah, who remains elusive after a traumatic incident. Swarm focuses on Dre’s extreme, compulsive fandom and how her desperate attempts to follow her desires lead her down a murderous path across the country. Rory Culkin, Paris Jackson, X Mayo, Billie Eilish, Stephen Glover, and more appear as guest stars.

A heavily underrated and often misunderstood psychological thriller, Swarm works both as a depiction of toxic obsession and a cautionary tale, anchored by Fishback’s menacing antagonist. The show is a disorienting blend of dark satire, gory slasher, and psychological horror. The series refuses to fit into any genre, shifting from graphic violence to true-crime mockumentary and surreal satire. Critics widely praise the show for being as disturbing as it is nuanced, and Fishback’s outstanding performance earned her multiple accolades, making Swarm one of the best shows about obsessive fandom.

In his first television show as a creator, director, and showrunner, Barry Jenkins adapts Colson Whitehead’s Pulitzer Prize-winning novel of the same name into a thrilling historical fiction story. The Underground Railroad tells the story of Cora and Caesar, two enslaved people on a Georgia plantation who escape their ruthless owners and attempt to take a magical subterranean train to freedom, while being chased by a slave catcher. Thuso Mbedu stars as Cora, Aaron Pierre as Caesar, and Joel Edgerton as the slave catcher.

Alternative history and magic realism come together in this haunting and thrilling story of survival and freedom, underscored by a great cast and an incredible visual style that demands uninterrupted attention. Barry Jenkins transports his theatrical storytelling style to the small screen, bringing life to Whitehead’s critically lauded bestseller that reimagines the titular network of abolitionists and their real-life efforts to help enslaved African-Americans escape to freedom. Even though it was well-acclaimed at its release and won several prestigious awards, The Underground Railroad is an underrated miniseries that deserves a lot more attention.

Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s critically acclaimed, multi-award-winning tragicomedy series that catapulted her to global recognition, Fleabag is a first-person narrative of the titular narrator’s personal tragedies, identity crisis, and difficult family dynamics. The 30-something single woman in London juggles her struggling café business and the deaths of her loved ones, giving the audience a darkly funny peek into her intimate emotions and challenges as she navigates romance, heartbreak, family drama, and loss. Besides Waller-Bridge, Andrew Scott also gained popularity as The Priest, while Sian Clifford, Brett Gelman, and Olivia Colman are also memorable for their roles.

Widely considered a television masterpiece of the past decade, Fleabag is pure comedic genius. Anchored by Waller-Bridge's pitch-perfect delivery, with a close second by Scott and Clifford, it is a wholesome, honest show that handles delicate themes like suppressed grief and identity crisis with more humor and heart in its limited runtime than multi-season television phenomena. Even though the show is split into two seasons, it is essentially one limited series divided into two chapters, which collectively tells a complete, single-arc story about the protagonist’s healing process that you will want to binge in one sitting.

#3380. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3379. New Doctor Doom Appearance Solves A Major Avengers: Doomsday Mystery (& Raises 2 Huge Questions)

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for VisionQuest episode 8

Doctor Doom's latest MCU appearances essentially confirm one of the biggest Avengers: Doomsday theories. However, there are still two fairly big question marks that are well worth discussing in the aftermath.

Between the multiverse's growing instability and the return of several familiar heroes from across realities, there are plenty of unanswered questions surrounding RDJ's Doctor Doom and his full plans for the multiverse. To that end, every new Doctor Doom appearance before Doomsday makes his plan all the more intriguing.

Following Doctor Doom's incredibly exciting appearance at the end of VisionQuest, it now seems more than likely that the ruler of Latveria will have a major ally by his side: Wanda Maximoff's Scarlet Witch. That being said, one still has to wonder who else might be supporting Doom's bid for power in Avengers: Doomsday.

As seen in VisionQuest's major post-credits scene, it was revealed that Doctor Doom revived and took Wanda Maximoff from Mount Wundagore after she brought the mountain down on herself at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, sacrificing herself to destroy every copy of the Darkhold in existence across realities.

Commanding Wanda to awaken in VisionQuest's second post-credits scene, Doctor Doom says that Wanda's power will become his before reviving her. By all accounts, this is a pretty important scene across the board before Doomsday. Not only does it confirm that Doom is amassing all kinds of power (like claiming the Hulk in one of Avengers: Endgame Encore post-credits scenes), it suggests quite a bit, considering what we already know about Doctor Doom and witches. After all, various promotional materials have shown Doctor Doom backed by a trio of mysterious masked women known only as the "Latverian Witches" throughout Avengers: Doomsday's marketing.

It stands to reason after VisionQuest that one of these Latverian Witches is Wanda herself, especially when you factor in the comics precedent with the "Children's Crusade" storyline, where Wanda went missing following her major House of M breakdown, only to be taken in by Doctor Doom who planned to marry the amnesiac Scarlet Witch in a bid to claim her power. Keeping that in mind, perhaps Wanda will similarly find herself serving Doom in Avengers: Doomsday, willingly or otherwise. However, there are still some pretty big questions about whom the other two Latverian witches might be.

Even before VisionQuest, Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch was a major candidate for one of Doctor Doom's masked Latverian Witches alongside Charlize Theron's Clea and Sophia Di Martino's Sylvie, especially with their differently colored (perhaps corresponding?) red, purple, and green robes. While Wanda is practically a foregone conclusion at this point, neither Clea nor Sylvie has been officially confirmed as a Latverian Witch.

Then again, an even wilder possibility is that all the Latverian Witches could be variants of Wanda Maximoff from across various realities. Perhaps Doom is collecting more than one Scarlet Witch in an effort to amplify his own power to absolutely massive levels.

That said, the distinct costume colors and the possibility of recruiting even more established magic users in the MCU make Clea and Sylvie the far more exciting/compelling answer.

Ultimately, Marvel Studios has yet to reveal who's beneath the other masks. Even so, with Wanda Maximoff's Scarlet Witch seemingly confirmed as one of Doom's witches, the mystery behind the other two mysterious magic wielders in Avengers: Doomsday just got way more exciting. All in all, it's going to be absolutely fascinating to learn what Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom intends for the collapsing multiverse, and how these witches in his service will factor into those plans. Thankfully, we won't have to wait much longer, with Avengers: Doomsday being just a few weeks away.

Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18th from Marvel Studios.

Avengers: Doomsday is the fifth Avengers film and kicks off Phase 6 of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. A stacked cast of heroes both new and old to the MCU — including members of the X-Men — will face off against Victor von Doom, revealed at San Diego Comic-Con in 2024 to be played by a returning Robert Downey Jr.

#3378. Apple TV launches new sign language accessibility feature

Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies.

The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later.

Alongside those two films, Apple said that sign language options will be available for Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid later this year, with more to come.

To access the new functionality, you need to be using the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad or Mac running 27.2 or later. The feature will also be available on some versions of the Apple TV app on other platforms.

By default, the Sign Language controls are hidden. If you want to use the feature, firstly go to the Settings app -> TV app, and enable the Sign Language display.

Then, on eligible titles, a new Sign Language button will appear in the player controls. You can simply toggle to enable, and choose from American Sign Language or British Sign Language modes.

When enabled, a signing interpreter then appears in the corner of the frame, synced with the video playback.

When browsing the catalog, sign language availability will also be shown next to the usual subtitle and audio language information. Users will also be able to search “with ASL” or “with BSL” to find compatible titles.

#3377. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

#3376. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.
