#3374. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3372. Netflix’s 6-Part Miniseries Brings One of the Greatest Novels of All Time to Life

Taylor Vollman is a contributor at Collider. She has long quipped, “T.V. is my name, TV is my game.” Fortuitous initials aside, at the heart of a tired joke is a simple truth — she has a lifelong passion for television. And along with it, an affinity for movies, music and pop culture.

In a childhood time capsule, she had listed Friends, PB&J Otter, and Days of Our Lives among her favorite shows. But her tastes have not narrowed with age. Her viewing habits span TV Land classics, network hits, buzzy reality shows and streamer critical darlings.

Hoping to merge this passion with her love of writing, Taylor earned a bachelor’s in media arts and design with a minor in film studies from James Madison University. After working in marketing for years, she wanted to sharpen her skills and went on to graduate with a master’s in journalism from Georgetown University. Taylor has since pursued entertainment writing and reporting.

Jane Austen is one of the preeminent romance authors of all time, giving her heroines a sense of agency when their fates largely depended on the men in their lives. Her stories have been finding new life in recent years, with romance readers driving an uptick in the genre across mediums. Netflix is no stranger to historical romance, behind the hit Bridgerton franchise and previously adapting Austen’s Persuasion in 2022. Now, the streaming platform is returning to the author’s most successful work, Pride and Prejudice. It was Austen’s second novel to be published, released in 1813.

Dolly Alderton was tapped to adapt the classic novel into a six-episode miniseries, following Elizabeth “Lizzy” Bennet (Emma Corrin) and Mr. Fitzwilliam Darcy (Jack Lowden) as they clash against their social station, ego, and misconceptions on their journey to love. Meddling elders, long-standing friendships, and secretive rivalries only threaten their happiness. Olivia Colman, Rufus Sewell, Freya Mavor, Rhea Norwood, Hopey Parish, and Hollie Avery round out the Bennet family. Hot off another Austen adaptation, Sense and Sensibility, Fiona Shaw stars as Lady Catherine de Bourgh. The cast also includes Jamie Demetriou, Daryl McCormack, Louis Partridge and Siena Kelly.

Pride and Prejudice continues to be relevant, even centuries after its publication. And while Alderton promises a faithful adaptation, she admits they reanalyzed some moments for the modern audience. The Good Material author admitted that age gave her a different perspective on the characters. “The thing that I was most drawn to as a single 35-year-old woman was how much Lizzy feels like a woman who is thinking out loud, who is trying to work out what she feels about marriage and love — what it is that she wants, what she’s willing to negotiate on,” Alderton explained to Netflix. This exploration of pragmatism in conversations with marriage is a relatable topic, even amid the modern dating landscape.

Lizzy is, in particular, a character open to a life without marriage, admitting in the trailer her willingness to be "a governess and a spinster." Corrin discussed the miniseries’ ability to interject a modern sensibility into its historical setting. “I don’t think we’ve had an adaptation that does the modernity and the authenticity that we love,” they told Netflix. “Some of the actual social commentary that comes out is really brilliant.”

Mrs. Bennet (Colman) is a complicated figure for many fans, who see her preoccupation with marriage as an inevitability of the era but a hindrance to her relationships. But she will be the first to speak the novel’s iconic opening line in an adaptation, “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” Originally just narration, Alderton explained that Mrs. Bennet speaks the famous line as it’s “the central drama of her story.” “It’s a preoccupation that any time a single man comes into her orbit, she’s thinking this might be safety for one of my daughters,” she explains while breaking down the trailer. “This might be salvation, not just for one but for all of us. So, the fact that this is so in her mind all the time, it felt that it had to be her line.”

Netflix is not just bringing Pride and Prejudice to a new generation, but is also reaffirming its literary status. It “is the ultimate romantic comedy,” as Netflix executive Mona Qureshi said in an announcement. Austen’s best-selling novel continues to appear on lists of the medium’s best, with The Guardian ranking it third among its “Readers’ top 100 novels of all time” and Goodreads ranking it first among the “Best Books of the 19th Century.”

As any casual shopper in a bookstore knows, Pride and Prejudice is frequently re-released as special editions. In fact, it has continually stayed in print and sold more than 20 million copies in the 213 years since its publication, according to Jane Austen’s House. And if the idiom about imitation is correct, Austen should be very flattered thanks to the many remakes and spinoffs it inspired.

Netflix unveils the official trailer and new images for its 6-part ‘Pride and Prejudice’ adaptation.

Netflix’s upcoming miniseries is entering an ongoing war over the best Pride and Prejudice adaptation, with an expansive multiverse of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy love stories. It has been adapted for stage, television, film, and even the Emmy-winning web series The Lizzie Bennet Diaries. But fans are most ardently divided between the 1995 miniseries starring Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle, and the 2005 film featuring Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen.

Austen’s work continues to be adapted, retold, and reimagined, with even literary retellings and spinoffs finding their way to screen. In fact, the modernized Bridget Jones’s Diary starring Renée Zellweger, the horror reimagining of Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, and Death Comes To Pemberley led by Matthew Rhys were all novels first. Most recently, BBC and BritBox brought the story of Mary (Ella Bruccoleri) to life in The Other Bennet Sister, which includes an upcoming 3-part Christmas special.

With the resurgence of romance, it only makes sense Netflix would adapt such a classic novel by a beloved author. Pride and Prejudice is a story told over and over again, recontextualized for each generation. Alderton promises to breathe new life into a timeless tale, even including an iconic line for the first time. The 6-part miniseries premieres on Netflix on December 3, 2026.

#3371. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3370. Elden Ring's Official Replacement Releasing In 2027

Elden Ring officially launched back in 2022, and since then, fans have wanted something new. Sure, there was the game-sized DLC that introduced a wealth of new content and was even considered a contender for Game of the Year. However, while Shadow of the Erdtree was so good that the Game Awards changed its rules to include it as a GOTY nominee, it too eventually became a tad stale. Of course, that is no fault of its own, but rather simply a consequence of the passage of time.

Naturally, people have turned to games like Elden Ring, although they are few and far between, and even those that exist fail to hold a candle to the original's excellence. Fortunately, after all this waiting, there is finally an official replacement for Elden Ring, and it is releasing sooner than you'd think. Scheduled to launch in 2027, this new game is set to be the next best Elden Ring-like, a tough feat to accomplish, but one that it is absolutely capable of achieving.

FromSoftware's next game, The Duskbloods, is set to be released in 2027. The Duskbloods' surprise delay pushed it out of its intended 2026 release window, something that perhaps comes as little surprise considering that, were it to release within the next two months, it would be contending with the likes of Grand Theft Auto 6. The decision was made as a consequence of the recent Duskbloods network test, which saw the developer receive a flurry of feedback from fans.

The Duskbloods has always been seen as Elden Ring's replacement ever since it was first announced. Its continuation of the open-world setting, coupled with its visual style and focus on multiplayer, feels like a blend between Elden Ring and its co-op spin-off, Nightreign. That is, of course, a good thing, especially as it means that FromSoftware isn't deviating too wildly from the formula that fans have come to know and love, much like it did with the release of the equally excellent Armored Core 6: Fires of Rubicon.

The only caveat is that The Duskbloods is a Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive. Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game's director, approached Nintendo with the loose idea for The Duskbloods, after which it began production, first as a Switch exclusive, and then as a Switch 2 exclusive after Nintendo requested a hardware change. While Elden Ring's Switch 2 port has performed well and thus has stirred up demand for a suitable replacement on that platform, it is obviously a shame that other platforms won't get to experience it.

Of course, it is possible that The Duskbloods will be a timed exclusive and eventually be ported to other platforms. FromSoftware does, after all, own the rights to it. However, as Nintendo is likely funding the exclusive, or at least has a contractual agreement with FromSoftware, this won't happen for a long time, if at all. Still, it is good that Elden Ring's official successor and ultimate replacement is finally on its way, even after a slight delay and a few bumps along the road to release.

#3368. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

It’s a small, flat, puck-shaped Bluetooth speaker that weighs just over half a pound, with a removable rubber strap you can attach to a backpack, bike handlebar, or shower caddy. The sale price is easier to justify when you consider that this is a new 2026 model. #3366. New Apple TV 4K remote’s best feature requires a newer iPhone model

A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

If you’re interested in the new Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

The most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

You can use the new Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the new speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the new Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

Will this limitation impact your Siri Remote purchase decision? Let us know in the comments.

#3364. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3362. 9 Agatha Christie Books To Read Before Kicking the Bucket

Beatriz (Bea) Valero de Urquia is a Books & Literature author at Collider, where she focuses on Lists surrounding recent bestsellers, classical novels, and everything in between. She is a historian by training and a bilingual reader, moving between English and Spanish literature.   Beatriz began her career as a technology writer at a startup in the UK. Almost a decade later, journalism has taken her to five cities across three continents and into business reporting, cultural criticism, and live TV commentary. She joined Collider in 2026.  Beatriz has a passion for travelling and loves keeping an eye on the books headed to the screen. One of her favorite pastimes is critiquing the historical accuracy of period movies. She also once volunteered for the Charles Dickens Museum. Beatriz also has a core belief that a book is always better than the movie, but she has been happy to have been proven wrong in a couple of occasions.

When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research. She enjoys tracing family trees for her history and genealogy TikTok, creating databases for historical analysis and sifting through 17th-century stories for the novel she is currently in the process of writing.

There are few pleasures that beat sitting on a couch in winter with a murder mystery, and everyone knows who writes them best. Agatha Christie is the best-selling novelist of all time. Her stories have only been outsold by the works of William Shakespeare and The Bible. Nicknamed "The Queen of Crime", Christie has been admired and beloved by people of every age for over a century. New adaptations of her novels come out every few years, from BBC's period dramas to Kenneth Branagh's most recent star-studded blockbusters. Currently, a six-part TV adaptation titled Hercule is in production by the BBC and BritBox, in which Edward Bluemel stars as a younger version of the famous fictional detective, Hercule Poirot.

But, where to start? Christie loved to write. Over her life, she published about 66 novels, 14 short story collections, around 25 play scripts, an autobiography and six romantic dramas under the pseudonym of Mary Westmacott. There is plenty of material to keep anyone busy every time they face a reading slump, or for many a winter season. Still, within all of these writings, there are some that are so essential that they should be on anyone’s bucket list. This compilation offers the essential Christie guide, from the best to the absolutely brilliant. The only thing missing is who did it.

Feeling intimidated? In that case, watching one of Agatha Christie's plays or picking up one of her short stories might be the best place to start. Among them, there is no other like Witness for the Prosecution. First published in the magazine Flynn's in 1925, it became the centerpiece of a 1948 short story collection. Its success led Agatha Christie herself to adapt the story to the stage. The revival of this adaptation is still playing in London today — inside London County Hall, no less.

Few of Christie's stories take place during a trial. The important thing is to uncover the truth, legal details aside. In Witness for the Prosecution, the truth is trickier to find. The story begins with an arrest: young, handsome Leonard Vole is charged with the murder of Emily French, a wealthy old woman who has named him heir to her fortune. He asks his wife, Romaine, to testify in his trial. In a turn of events, Romaine agrees, but she testifies for the prosecution instead of the defense. With its twists and turns, the story has captivated a generation, even with its changing endings, different in the first installment of the story, in the play, in Billy Wilder's 1957 version, and in the 2016 two-part TV drama by BBC One that starred Kim Cattrall as Emily French.

For decades, readers could expect a brand-new Agatha Christie novel every holiday season. Her publisher even used the slogan "a Christie for Christmas" to sell more books. Hercule Poirot's Christmas, one of her few works centered around the holidays, was perhaps the bloodiest of her novels. Christie dedicated it to her brother-in-law, James Watts, who complained her murders were becoming too refined and "yearned for a good violent murder with lots of blood." She certainly delivered. If the Christmas season does not make you particularly jolly, or if you are tired of sickly-sweet seasonal stories, this is the book for you.

Hercules Poirot's Christmas holiday break is interrupted when he is called to investigate the death of the wealthy Simeone Lee. The multimillionaire had invited his four sons and their spouses to gather at his mansion for the holidays, alongside a granddaughter they had not met, and the son of a business partner. The family reunion is tense, taking place until Christmas Eve, when an awful scream echoes through the house, alongside sounds of furniture breaking. The noise is tracked down to be coming from the patriarch's locked room, where he is found dead in a pool of blood.

Do not read this book first. It is very important. Do not read it until after you have read every other Agatha Christie book out there, or at least those that surround her most famous and beloved character, Hercule Poirot and his dear friend Arthur Hastings. The story returns the reader to Styles Court in Essex, the scene of The Mysterious Affair at Styles, Poirot's first case in England. This time, the now-frail detective believes a murder is about to take place, by the same person that has already committed five others in that same place. Said and done. Still, Poirot is set on catching the killer.

Written in the preamble to WWII and during the London Blitz, Curtain is one of Agatha Christie's most serious novels. The author kept the manuscript locked away for years after writing it, and only allowed it to be published months before her own death in 1976. Its plot offers readers a deeper ethical puzzle, one not even the author gives a concrete answer to. Do not read this book first, but do read it at some point, because very few characters in fiction have conclusions to their stories that are as fascinating and well-executed as this one.

Agatha Christie loved a good nursery rhyme reference. In this case, she uses This Little Piggy as the framing device for a story about a 16-year-old murder. In the story, Hercule Poirot is asked to defend a deceased person. It starts when Carla Lemarchant receives a letter from her deceased mother, who had been convicted of poisoning her husband, Amyas Crale. In the letter, Carolina claims to be innocent. Carla then convinces Poirot to reexamine the case and investigate the five people who were present at the home the day Amyas died. With any evidence of the crime long gone, Poirot is forced to reconstruct the events of the murder from the witnesses' memories in a magnificent psychological exercise.

The five suspects remind Poirot of the five little piggies of the nursery rhyme. The pig that "went to market" is stockbroker Philip Blake. His brother, herbalist Meredith Blake, is the one who stayed home. Three-times divorcee Elsa Greer is the pig who "had roast beef," while devoted governess Cecilia Williams "had none." Finally, Angela Warren, Amyas' daughter and Carla's half-sister, "cried wee wee all the way home." Following the pattern of the rhyme, the book allows each character to tell their version of what happened that day, until the truth is finally revealed.

Toni Collette and Kit Harington are shooting a new Miss Marple and 20th Century has several more Christies in development, so the drawing room is busier than it has been in decades. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best.

Order, method, and a quiet confidence that you are the cleverest person present. Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer who solves murders by sitting still and thinking, and who is vain enough to make the reveal a performance every single time.

People tell you things because they cannot imagine you being a threat. Marple solves murders by comparing everybody to somebody she once knew in St Mary Mead, which sounds like a joke until you notice it works every time, because human beings are not as original as they think.

You have far too many ideas and roughly a fifth of them are excellent. Ariadne Oliver is a successful crime novelist who is sick of her famous foreign detective and keeps saying so, which is Christie writing about Christie and getting away with it completely.

You are steady, decent and the reason the difficult genius has anybody at all. Hastings narrates the early Poirot novels, misses most of the clues, and is the only character in the books that Poirot is unambiguously fond of, which tells you what he is really for.

If there is one Agatha Christie story most readers are sure to know the ending of, it's Murder on the Orient Express. It is simply that timeless. And yet, it is still one that any fan of crime novels must pick up at one point in their lives. It presents Christie's most iconic group of characters, including the mysterious American businessman named Ratchett, his secretary, Hector MacQueen; American widow Mrs. Caroline Hubbard; Swedish missionary Greta Ohlsson; Italian-American car salesman Antonio Foscarelli; English colonel John Arbuthnot; Russian Princess Dragomiroff; and, of course, Belgian detective Hercule Poirot, among others. All of them find themselves aboard the luxurious Orient Express train. Then, someone dies. When the train is stopped due to a snowstorm, all the passengers and the murderer are trapped inside.

Partly inspired by the 1932 kidnapping of twenty-month-old Charles Augustus Lindbergh Jr., as well as Agatha Christie's own experience getting stuck on the Orient Express, the story is one told generation after generation. Its plot has been adapted several times, including the 1974 Sidney Lumet version and the more recent 2017 movie with Kenneth Branagh, as well as two video games, a comic and a 2015 Japanese-language movie. Murder on the Orient Express is inescapable, yet it still stands the test of time.

"A murder is announced and will take place on Friday, October 29th at Little Paddocks at 6:30 p.m." This is the message that the residents of a small village find in the local newspaper one morning like any other. The notice is a surprise even to Miss Letitia Blacklock, the woman whose home has been identified as the future crime scene. Intrigued, several villagers show up at the time indicated. When the clock strikes 6:30, the lights go out and a door opens, revealing a masked man. He screams. Shots follow. When the light returns, a bullet has grazed Miss Blacklock's ear and the man is dead. He is later identified as Rudi Scherz, a Swiss receptionist at a local spa.

Leaving Poirot's "little gray cells" to rest for a while, this book features Miss Jane Marple. The woman's favorite pastimes include gardening, knitting and birdwatching. Oh, and who could forget solving crimes? Miss Marple happens to be a guest at the spa where Scherz had been working, and so Inspector Craddock decides to involve her in the investigation. Joan Hickson, Christie's own preferred choice to play the role, starred as Miss Marple in the BBC's 1985 adaptation. A Murder Is Announced is widely considered the best Miss Marple case, a fascinating psychological portrait and a poignant portrayal of the postwar era in the English countryside. It was Agatha Christie's 50th novel and a sign that her talent knew no bounds.

Cruises can be deadly, even for the luckiest of people. Wealthy, beautiful and young Linnet Doyle is the picture of the perfect bride, celebrating an even more perfect honeymoon in Egypt with her husband, Simon Doyle. No one pays much notice to the fact that he had previously been engaged to Linnet's former best friend, Jacqueline de Bellefort. No one, until Jacqueline herself shows up aboard the same Nile River cruise Linnet and Simon are on. She is bound to be the prime suspect when Linnet appears dead. Except, she could not have done it. How lucky then, that Hercule Poirot happened to also be a passenger on the ship, and is set to solve the mystery.

Death on the Nile is Christie at her most glamorous and exotic. Instead of taking place in the English countryside, the story transports the reader into a luxurious boat and into the temples of Abu Simbel. Equally beautiful is the photography for the 2022 adaptation of the story, directed by Kenneth Branagh and starring Gal Gadot as Linnet, Emma Mackey as Jacqueline, and Armie Hammer as Simon. The story's ending is one of the most consequential of all of Christie's. With jealousy, friendship and romance as its themes, it is truly a story about obsession, set in a location that has obsessed humanity for millennia.

It is difficult to explain what makes The Murder of Roger Ackroyd so outstanding as a murder mystery without giving away its ending. Just believe me. Suffice to say, it is often considered Christie's masterpiece and, in 2013, the British Crime Writers' Association voted it the best crime novel in history. This is all as a result of its final twist, which made it one of the author's most controversial stories.

Meet Dr James Sheppard. He is the local physician of King's Abbot, a small English village, as well as the story's narrator. Dr Sheppard lives a life that "never (has) anything out of the ordinary" until he is asked to certify the death of the wealthy widow Mrs Ferrars. Rumors claimed Mrs Ferrars had poisoned her own husband and ended her life out of remorse. It made sense to everyone, except Roger Ackroyd, a wealthy widower who was engaged to her. Ackroyd knows she was being blackmailed but, just as he is about to read the letter that contains the identity of the blackmailer, he is murdered in his study. Secrets slowly unravel, building up to an ending that shatters all the rules of detective fiction. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd paved the way for Gone Girl, Memento, and The Silent Patient.

Ten people are gathered on a remote island. Upon arrival, a message recorded on a gramophone accuses all of them of being responsible for someone's death. On the dinner table, there are ten figurines and an old nursery rhyme is framed in each room. Once the recording ends, one of the guests, Anthony Marston, finishes his drink and dies from cyanide poisoning. The next morning, Mrs. Rogers is found dead in her bed. Slowly, the guests continue to die, with each death echoing a line of the rhyme. After each passing, one figurine disappears from the table, like a slow tic tac that warns the remaining guests of their impending fate.

And Then There Were None is a work of art when murder mysteries are concerned. With no detective in sight, it is up to the guests to investigate each other while trying to keep themselves alive. In a way, it is also the Russian doll of whodunnits. In addition to figuring out the person who is killing the guests, the reader is also compelled to discover each character's backstory and the death each of them is responsible for. Agatha Christie considered it a better piece of craftsmanship than anything else she had written. She took on the writing "because it was so difficult to do that the idea fascinated me." Now, it fascinates the world.

#3361. Star Trek: Shadow Frontier Is Finally Giving An Underrated Next Generation Character Their Time To Shine

Star Trek has been around for an astounding 60 years, and we don't really know where it's going to go next. After a brand-new era that kicked off with five seasons of Star Trek: Discovery, Trek came back in a big way with Picard, Lower Decks, Prodigy, Strange New Worlds, and Starfleet Academy, plus a ton of other projects.

That includes games and spinoffs, some of which are still set for release. Now, as we enter an uncertain era for the series with no mainline entry in development, an underrated Star Trek character is set to shine in the near future.

Developed by Bloober Team and published by Paramount Games, Star Trek: Shadow Frontier is looking to deliver a completely new experience for Star Trek fans on Steam, and one you don't see very often. This is a story-centric horror game from Paramount Games, and it looks like it's going to pack a punch according to the official description:

"Star Trek: Shadow Frontier is a story-driven, action-adventure set in the expansive Star Trek universe. Step into the fractured mind of former Lieutenant Ro Laren (voiced by Michelle Forbes) as she seeks to rescue an old friend by embarking on a harrowing journey of survival and self-discovery. In true Star Trek fashion, Ro’s mission is driven by duty and purpose. But here, discovery comes at a terrible cost. The more she uncovers, the deeper she is pulled into a corrupted labyrinth where her memories twist, and the planet threatens to sever her connection to reality."

The idea is that you'll play as Ro and confront her demons while venturing into the darkness (and the Star Trek universe can get pretty dark at times). This time you're investigating a lethal planet, including "weaponized" creatures, which you'll need to either fight or flee from as you explore.

The ecosystem is also described as "hostile" (Shadow Frontier indeed), and will even try to absorb Ro's consciousness and haunt her mind, similar to any number of hallucination-delivering supervillains. Thankfully, you'll have access to a Tricorder to scan objects and a Phaser to defend yourself. The "psychological action-adventure" doesn't have a release date yet, but it is in development and warns players against "intense violence, blood and gore."

Ro Laren was introduced in Star Trek: The Next Generation, and is a Bajoran who Jean-Luc Picard reluctantly works with at first. She joined the show in the fifth season, and like any given character in Star Trek history, she has plenty of fans.

She was originally portrayed by Michelle Forbes, who reprises her role in Shadow Frontier. This degree of authenticity is pretty huge for Star Trek fans, who often see the original portrayals as the canon versions of those characters.

The render of Ro in Star Trek: Shadow Frontier is faithful to her likeness, and the original performer is set to return, so the game sounds great on paper so far. Plus, given Bloober Team's recent success with the Silent Hill 2 remake and Cronos: The New Dawn, they're continuing to cement themselves as a go-to for modern horror.

Woot has dropped the price of the JBL PartyBox 330 to $479.95 as an early Black Friday deal, saving you $150 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. For comparison, the same speaker currently costs $629.95 at Amazon, although that purchase includes a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music. Woot, meanwhile, offers free shipping for Prime members ($6 otherwise), and covers the new unit with a 90-day limited warranty.

Beyond the discount, the PartyBox 330 has plenty to offer if you're looking for a speaker that can handle everything from backyard barbecues to larger gatherings—sitting between the smaller Club 120 and the larger PartyBox 520 in JBL's lineup, it delivers deep, punchy bass and enough volume to entertain a crowd, while its roughly 20-hour battery life means you can keep the music going all day without having to find an outlet. It's also rated IPX4 for water resistance, so a little rain or an accidental splash shouldn't be a problem.

That protection has limits, though—the 330 isn’t dustproof or particularly impact-resistant, so you’ll still want to be careful where you set it down. Audio-wise, sound quality also changes depending on where you're standing, with music becoming noticeably more muffled from the sides and behind. Fortunately, JBL's graphic equalizer and sound presets give you some control over the tuning. The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

Apple is working on a new app called HarborHarbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf

As the post notes, here’s what the app does:

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.

#3357. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3356. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

The "I Know What You Did Last Summer" star and "Get Out" actor were interviewed by NBC 16 in Eugene, Oregon, as they waited for the nationwide ground stop to be lifted.

Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.

#3353. 6 Netflix Movies With the Highest Rotten Tomatoes Scores, Ranked

In the modern age of filmmaking, it's impossible to deny the influence and overwhelming popularity that streaming services have held as one of the main ways that many modern audiences experience film, whether it be an array of classics from the past or some of the hottest new releases. However, it comes down to the original content that a streaming service offers in terms of distinguishing itself from the competition, with no other streaming service coming close to the impact and outright memorability of Netflix's offerings.

In terms of original films especially, Netflix is leaps and bounds ahead of its competition, largely thanks to how wide of a net that the studio casts in terms of financing and distributing just about every type of film imaginable. When at their best, Netflix original films can be some of the most acclaimed films of their respective years and must-watch phenomena that continue to be appreciated years after their release. While there are many different methods to discern the best and most celebrated films Netflix has released, the Rotten Tomatoes score paints a picture of widespread appeal and praise for these films.

The romantic comedy genre largely saw a downswing during the early 2010s, simply not being able to compete with the likes of massive romance blockbusters while the truly passionate and artistic rom-coms of the era aimed for a more niche, indie audience. However, Netflix has largely become one of the most pervasive forces for the return to prominence of rom-coms, especially teenage rom-coms, with the driving force for this return to form being To All the Boys I've Loved Before.

It may seem silly that this seemingly simple teenage rom-com has such a massive Rotten Tomatoes score, but it speaks volumes not only to how effectively the film plays into classic rom-com archetypes, but also just how starved many critics and audiences of the late 2010s were for a classic rom-com experience. The film soars due to an abundance of charm, largely thanks to the dynamic and chemistry between leads Lana Condor and Noah Centineo, as well as a quaint setup that helps with the inherent memorability of the film.

The latest cinematic masterpiece from legendary director Alfonso Cuarón, Roma is a strikingly beautiful portrait of emotional hardships that plays with the audience's heartstrings with tactful precision. This Spanish-language film was the definitive must-watch indie film of 2018 and has stood as one of the premier examples of how Netflix is capable of releasing striking and beautiful works of cinematic art. It became the first Netflix original film to be nominated for Best Picture, as well as arguably being the closest that the platform has been to actually winning the legendary award.

It simply goes without saying that Cuarón's masterpiece of black-and-white filmmaking was a massive hit with critics and audiences alike, with Roma being a once-in-a-generation work of art that spoke to the potential of the cinema in the streaming era. It's far from the only critically acclaimed film that Netflix has put out, but the massive amounts of prestige and passion surrounding the film showed they are more than just a streaming platform — rather, they are a genuine competitor and provider of artistic cinematic brilliance.

All of the pieces were there for Ma Rainey's Black Bottom to be a massive critical success, becoming a massively beloved love letter to 1920s blues music that defined the 2020 awards season but was sadly forgotten due to being snubbed for Best Picture. While its passionate musical story and how it balances the drama surrounding Blues culture in the '20s is great enough, the real selling point and impact of the film comes from its legendary central performances.

Chadwick Boseman, in his final film role, absolutely steals the show in what is largely considered the best performance of his career, while Viola Davis matches this energy and further elevates the dramatic weight of the film. Between these outstanding performances and the overall lack of competition in prestigious films in the midst of the pandemic, it isn't exactly surprising that critics of the era flocked to the film and were quick to sing its many praises.

While Netflix has acted as a dominating force that has revitalized and completely transformed many different genres during its tenure, crime documentaries are arguably one of the genres most overwhelmingly changed by Netflix's influence. The platform is constantly releasing high-profile documentaries that bolster its reputation as a source for hard-hitting cinematic journalism, although even with many great docs released, they don't hold a candle to the brilliance and power of Sundance darling The Perfect Neighbor.

This emotional and painful story of real-life violence and murder in a small Florida community makes massive statements by largely showing how it transpired without much change. It tells its story entirely through bodycam footage, painting a picture both through what is directly seen by law enforcement and the implications and pain implied through what is seen. The film saw overwhelming acclaim after it premiered at Sundance, leading Netflix to acquire the film and add it to its repertoire of massively acclaimed documentaries.

Compared to the films that have received multitudes of awards or overwhelming popularity on the platform, Under the Shadow overwhelmingly sticks out among the critical darlings that Netflix has released over the years. However, this emotional wartime supernatural horror film is absolutely deserving of its 99% Tomatometer score, bringing to life an incredibly abstract and intricate concept and utilizing it perfectly for its haunting themes of social terror and systemic misogyny.

It's an outright perfect horror movie that most people simply haven't heard of, but its critical reception paints the entire picture of just how much of a hidden gem Under the Shadow is. The film follows a mother and daughter who begin being haunted by a mysterious apparition that they believe may have entered their home after their building was struck by a missile during the Iran-Iraq War. Convinced of the danger of these supernatural forces, this mother will have to face them head-on in order to protect her daughter.

In terms of icon status mixed with an overwhelming abundance of charm and whimsy, it's hard to beat the consistency of Aardman's Wallace & Gromit. This placed all sorts of expectations on their glorious return to feature-length filmmaking after 19 years of absence, with Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl fully living up to the reputation of the franchise in the eyes of critics. In the process, it ended up being Netflix's only film to have achieved an unbreakable 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes.

It is certainly a bit silly that this illustrious achievement is held by a children's animated film, but it's impossible to conceive of even a single person who wouldn't crack a smile at the stop-motion charm of one of animation's greatest duos. Vengeance Most Fowl acts as a glorious continuation of everything that made this duo so iconic in the first place, amplifying their charms and sticking with what makes them great while also tapping into concerns of the modern age with a satirical anti-AI message. There's certainly the possibility for Netflix to release another film that achieves a 100% on Rotten Tomatoes in the future, but for the time being, the mantle will have to be maintained by the UK's favorite man-and-dog duo.
